query: For the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets that are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain why their mechanical properties differ during deformation and failure when constituent count alone is inadequate? Specify a controlled comparison, predictions relative to the quinary baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy develops chemically modulated mesoscopic domains (local short‐range chemical ordering) during thermomechanical processing that act as strong obstacles to dislocation motion. In contrast, the quaternary and ternary subsets, lacking one or more critical elements (notably Cr or Mn), form these ordered domains to a lesser extent. As a result, the quinary alloy exhibits enhanced strain hardening and distinct deformation/failure behavior compared to its lower‐constituent counterparts.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase FCC structure obtained by identical thermomechanical processing for the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its quaternary and ternary subsets.
generation.intervention: Conduct controlled mechanical deformation tests (e.g., tensile tests) on samples of the quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys under identical processing history and deformation conditions.
generation.conditions: Deformation tests conducted under identical strain rates and temperatures (including room temperature and elevated temperatures where dislocation activity dominates) while ensuring comparable grain sizes and microstructures.
generation.structural_mediator: Chemically modulated mesoscopic domains (local chemical short-range orders) that can be detected by techniques such as synchrotron small-angle diffraction.
generation.mechanism: In the fully complex quinary alloy, the multi-element interactions promote the formation of mesoscale chemical ordering. These domains impede dislocation motion and alter dynamic strain hardening (as seen via changes in electrical resistivity—the K-effect), leading to differences in deformation and failure. The lower complexity alloys form fewer or smaller such domains, resulting in less dislocation obstruction and altered mechanical responses.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will show a lower strain hardening rate and smaller changes in electrical resistivity during plastic deformation. Synchrotron small-angle diffraction should reveal reduced intensity or absence of mesoscopic domain signals in these alloys.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni (quinary) alloy, exhibiting pronounced mesoscopic domains that correlate with enhanced mechanical resistance during deformation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies only to single-phase FCC structures produced by comparable thermomechanical processing and when deformation is dominated by dislocation-mediated plasticity rather than other mechanisms such as twinning or phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain whether other factors (e.g., subtle differences in grain size, residual stresses, or nano-precipitate formation) might also contribute to the observed differences in mechanical behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate equiatomic samples of the quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys ensuring identical thermomechanical processing parameters. Use synchrotron small-angle diffraction to quantify the presence and size of mesoscopic domains before and after deformation. Perform tensile tests under the same strain rate and temperature conditions while measuring strain hardening rates and in situ electrical resistivity.
measurements: Synchrotron small-angle diffraction intensity and peak broadening (indicative of mesoscopic domains)
Microstructural analysis (electron backscatter diffraction, TEM) to monitor dislocation configurations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the quinary alloy does not exhibit a significantly greater formation (or dissolution) of mesoscopic domains relative to its quaternary and ternary subsets, or if the measured mechanical responses (strain hardening and electrical resistivity changes) do not correlate with the presence of these domains, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
Chemically modulated mesoscopic domains in a fcc single phase CrMnFeCoNi equi-atomic high entropy alloy (HEA) are detected by small angle diffraction performed at a synchrotron radiation facility, whereas the mesoscopic domains cannot be detected by conventional X-ray diffraction and 2D mappings of energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy by scanning electron microscopy and scanning transmission electron microscopy. The mesoscopic domains are deformed and shrieked, and finally destructed by plastic deformation, which is supported by the comprehensive observations/measurements, such as electrical resistivity, Vickers hardness, electron backscattering diffraction, and hard X-ray photoemission spectroscopy. The destruction of the mesoscopic domains causes the decrease in electrical resistivity via plastic deformation, so called K-effect, which is completely opposite to the normal trend of metals. We confirmed that the presence and the size of local chemical ordering or short-range order domains in the single phased HEA, and furthermore, Cr and Mn are related to form the domains.
